BALBO'S TAKING-OFF. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
New York, Aug. 6.—Pietro Balbo was hanged in the Tombs prison-yard at seventeen minutes past 8 o'clock this morning for the murder of his young wife Sept. 30, 1879. He announced his intention the night before of not going to bed, but a little after midnight he went to his cell with Father Ancelus and began to cry. After a short prayer, he throw himself upon his cot and slept restlessly until 3 o'clock, when he arose and prayed by himself. At 5:30 o'clock his counsel, Mr. Klutzing, arrived. The condemned man attended mass in the chapel at 6 o'clock, after which he returned to his cell. Soon afterward he knelt at the altar in his cell and asked for Divine mercy. At ten minutes to 8 o'clock a bowl of coffee was sent to him in his cell, which he drank. As soon as he drank it he turned to his counsel and said: "Where's Sheriff? Me want to go." Word was immediately sent to the Sheriff, and the noose and black cap being adjusted, the procession started in the following order: Sheriff Bowe, and Under-Sheriff Evans, the prisoner with his hands clasping a crucifix to his breast, supported on his right by Father Ancelus and on his left by Father Duranquet, while closing up the rank were William K. Klutzing and the Rev. Edward J. Morgan, of Massachusetts.

The procession moved slowly across the yard to the gallows. Balbo moved his lips as if in prayer, and walked quietly without seeming to observe anything which went on about him. As the little procession reached the gallows all knelt. As the condemned man dropped on his knees under the gallows and kissed the crucifix which he had through out held in his hand, he still prayed as he had done almost uninterruptedly for hours, and while the three priests continued their prayers a deputy stepped up and arranged the noose around his neck, and stepped back without pulling down the black cap. An outsider attracted his attention to the oversight, and the officer arranged the hat, and at seventeen minutes past 8 Assistant-Sheriff Stevens made the motion with his handkerchief which indicated to the nameless man at

the tr. all was ready, and the drop fell on the instant.

When the body had hung for three minutes the pulse at the wrist showed 100 beats a minute, but suddenly ceased two minutes later, when the body was lowered until the toes touched the ground. At twenty-six minutes after 8, nine minutes after the drop had fallen, the heart showed eighty pulsations a minute, but were very irregular. At half-past 8, when the body had hung only sixteen minutes, they had ceased entirely, and the condemned man was dead. Two minutes later the remains were lowered into the coffin, and the usual superficial post mortem examination was made. One of the smaller bones of the throat had been ruptured, but that had little to do with causing death, unless by an internal hemorrhage, which may have assisted the strangulation, whose time was unusually short. Its neck was dislocated by the fall, but the spinal cord was not ruptured.

The body will be buried in Calvary Cemetery to-morrow.

CASH KILLED.

CHARLOTTE, N. C., Aug. 6.—Much excitement has been created in the city to-day by passengers coming in on the Carolina Central train, who reported that a fatal duel had been fought in the Marlboro section of South Carolina between young Cash, a son of Col. Cash, who recently killed Col. Shannon, and Mr. Blair, editor of the Camden Journal. It is stated that young Cash was killed instantly. The information received here is that Cash challenged Blair because of certain condemnatory editorials in the Journal on the late Cash-Shannon duel, and that the combat was fought with Winchester rifles at twenty paces. Owing to the out-of-the-way situation of Camden it is impossible to verify the report to-night, and there is no telegraphic communication between hero and the Marlboro section.

Depatch to Cincinnati Gazette.

CHARLESTON, S. C., Aug. 5.—Cash, the murderer of Col. Shannon, and the present Regulator of the press of South Carolina, writes thus to the editor whom he attempted to pound a few days since:

Cash's Depot, July 22, 1880.—R. H. Pequier, Editor of the Carolina Sun: Your issue of this date has been received, and I hasten to reply to your article under the caption, "The Irrepressible Conflict." I am truly gratified to have an opportunity to explain to the people of Chesterfield, and especially to those residing in your town, the misunderstanding that admitted the trouble which occurred on Friday last. Soon after my sight with Col. Shannon you published an article which was wholly unjustifiable, misrepresenting most important facts and alluding to me in a most contemptuous manner. You charged me with having sent the challenge which led to the fight, and arrogantly remarked that you would leave me to "remorse and probably to the hands of the law."

What right, sir, did you have to dispose of me in that or any other manner? Could you have gone further in expressing your contempt? Is there one truthful and intelligent man in this State who will indorse your conduct? Editors, and some lawyers, seem to think they possess peculiar privileges, and have a right to assail with impunity the character of private individuals. This, sir, will not be admitted. Private individuals have rights, and among those rights is the right to protect and defend their characters and the characters of those who are near and dear to them. This, sir; is your "irrepressible conflict," the private citizen on one side and your privileged class on the other.

But, sir, to the explanation of the trouble on Friday, the 16th. A few days previous I met my lifelong friend, Capt. Mallory, who urged me to keep quiet, and have no difficulty with you at present. I supposed he spoke thus on account of the importance to me of being quiet. It never occurred to me that he in any manner represented you. I told him that I did not intend to make an issue with you at present. It did not occur to me that he might give you my words as a guarantee. If it had I should certainly have warned my son of the obligation, and he would most assuredly have kept it sacred. As it was, neither of us knew anything of the understanding between Capt. Mallory and yourself. It was not my purpose to attack you on Friday, and I am sure my son had no such thought one moment before the difficulty occurred. It was all the act of a moment, and without premeditation. I say this, not by way of palliation, but for a fair understanding. When the difficulty occurred I went forward, not to take part, but to enforce a fair fight, and so expressed myself at the time.

I regret this trouble from beginning to end. It is calculated to antagonize lifelong friends, sir, for among the most cherished friends I have are your kinsmen and relatives, and those who bear your name.

I hope this explanation will satisfy you and your friends as to my "broken word." And now, in the interest of peace, and good order, I propose that the past shall be forgotten. Respectfully,

E. B. CASH.

BLUFFTON, Ind., Aug. 5.—This is the seat of Wells County, a ballwick notorious for its ultra Democratic capabilities and doings. Bluffton is a place of over 2,000 inhabitants, but the spirit displayed by some of its hot-headed Democrats does not invite a flow of people into our midst. The citizens here have read much about the atrocities committed by the Ku-Klux of the South and the horrors of Yazoo, yet they (at least the moral, law-abiding citizens) have not suspected, up to within a few days at least, that there would be anything of that sort done here. Lately, however, the hot blood which has coursed the veins of the unerrified has bubbled a little too high, and work has really commenced on the Yazoo plan.

Several of our citizens have received notices from the determined Democrats to part with the negroes they retain, and to "do it d—d quick."

CINCINNATI, August 12.—Demeratic threats of driving the negroes out of Indiana are being put into execution in at least three counties.

Early yesterday morning a band of masked Kuklux attacked the house of an inoffensive negro named Joshua Mack, one mile from Columbus, Ind., broke open the door and windows, and dragged him from his bed, declaring with vile oaths that they would hang him, and that they intended to "clean out all the niggers in the county before the election." They ransacked the house for arms, and found none, and finally agreed to let Mack go on condition that he would immediately leave. After they had gone some distance he followed them into the road where others were waiting, when all mounted their horses and rode away. Soon after they had gone some distance he followed them into the road where others of the party were waiting, when all mounted their horses and rode away. Soon after the house of Mr. Walker, who has a farm rented on which the negro lives, was stoned, the party yelling, cursing, and threatening about it for a considerable time. At Bluffton and Shelbyville similar attempts at intimidation have been made.

PALESTINE, Tex., Aug. 27.—Great excitement has been caused here by the announcement that Roland Rucker, who was to have been hanged here to-day for the murder of R.P. Grayson and wife, had committed suicide. When the prison authorities visited his cell at 5 o'clock this morning they found the man in the last agonies of death. Near him was a large pool of blood, and blood was issuing from a wound in his left wrist, which he had made with a penknife. On examination it was found that the arteries had been severed. How Rucker got possession of the knife is a mystery.

KU-KLUXED THE WRONG NEGRO.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

CINCINNATI, O., Aug. 27.—A case of Ku-Kluxing with a happy termination occurred near Cochran, Ga., night before last. At midnight John Brown, a peaceable negro citizen, was aroused by the demands of two armed and disguised men for entrance. They declared they had come there to whip him. Brown replied that he was at home, but that he would not open the door, and would not be whipped. The men grew furious, fired at Brown twice, when he seized a shotgun and let them have two heavy loads of buckshot. Both fell dead, having received the charge in their heads. Brown recognized them as Frank and Mack Dykes, two young farmers with whom he recently had a difficulty about work. He notified the authorities, and a Coroner's Inquest was held over the bodies in the presence of a great crowd. The verdict declares that Brown acted only in self-defense, and a good portion of the public Indorse his course. Many citizens approve his pluck and promise him any assistance he may need.

A REMARKABLE CASE.
A party of bulldozers made a serious mistake in Georgia the other day. They went at midnight, armed and disguised, to commit an outrage upon a negro who had dared to think for himself in politics. They fired into his cabin and then burst in the door, whereupon their intended victim fired both barrels of a shotgun at them, and killed two on the spot. If there had been more negroes like this one bulldozing would have gone out of fashion long ago. The Coroner's jury held an inquest, and brought in a verdict of justifiable homicide. This is by far the most remarkable fact in the case. It is wonderful enough to find a colored man with the courage to resist oppression, but to find a Southern Coroner's jury willing to justify such an act of self-defense is at least sufficient to demonstrate that the exigencies of the campaign are beginning to be realized down South, and that an attempt is being made to act upon the "no killing" order from headquarters.

For the Freeman.
Suppose an honest inquirer after truth should attempt to trace out the causes which have contributed to forming the two great political parties of the country. Necessarily such inquirer would need to study the country's history very critically, and its constitution and laws as well. He would naturally go back to the origin of the government, even to preliminary proceedings to its formation; he would study with great care the discussions in the preliminary conventions of the states and the continental congress, to learn the immost thought of the fathers of the republic, that was to be.

By this search our inquirer will find that the honest old patriots of those days differed in their views of the details in the form of the government they wished to construct. It was to be one best possible to make, secure and perpetuate the freedom gained by the revolution. The men of that transitory period first tried confederation, a sort of league or alliance of the states, as a protection against foreign hostile powers or domestic or inter-state conflicts. "Jefferson's Notes of Debate on Confederation" are interesting to the curious inquirer.

For the convenience of the reader who is curious to learn the early history of the two great parties which now divide the people of this nation, we will refer him to the articles of confederation and their acknowledged defectiveness in securing the purpose and permanence of a national Union. These articles were useful as preliminary to the formation of the national constitution. The debates in the colonial conventions on these articles and the debates on the United States constitution in the state conventions of course disclosed a diversity of views entertained by the patriots and statesmen of those days. Just how the powers of government should be distributed between the states and general government was something of a problem, but how those powers should be so clearly defined in the national constitution that no disputes or mistakes should ever occur in the different departments of state and general government seems to have been quite as much a problem. From the different constructions of constitutional powers parties have originated. When the inquirer for the origin of the parties has read up "Jefferson's Notes of the Debates on Confederation" let him take up the debates in the national and state conventions for the adoption of the United States constitution. Among those delegated members were men of imperishable fame, but having diverse views as to some of the features to be incorporated into the constitution, and after it had been ultimately formed and submitted for final ratification there was doubtless diversity of opinions to the extent of some of its provisions.

However perfectly for imperfectly conflicting views might have been harmonized at the time it is evident that in a few years after different constructions of the respective powers of the general and state government began to be published on high authorities; for instance, on the part of strict construction and state sovereignty the famous Virginia and Kentucky resolutions of 1798 were promulgated as the views of those importaot states, Mr. Madison speaking for Virginia and Mr. Jefferson for Kentucky state rights doctrines.

The documents referred to above may be found in a valuable book published some twenty years ago, entitled, "Teachings of Patriots and Statesmen," compiled by E. B. Chase.

The doctrine of those resolutions, most evidently, is that of more modern state sovereignty; it cropped out notably in the threatened nullification of South Carolina in 1832, but the still more notable rebellion of 1861. After the close of that sanguinary war the friends of the Union fondly hoped that the pestilent political heresy of state sovereignty was silenced forever; but what do we now see in the political aspect of our country? Many of the leaders and most of the rank and file of the rebellion dictating congress and aspiring to seize the executive arm of the government, and with that, eventually to control the supreme judiciary of the nation. Shall this dictation of congress and aspiration to complete control of the nation be suffered to continue and succeed? That is the great issue made up for the American people to decide within a few short weeks now, and may be forever.

In conclusion, were there time and space to go into detail, it might be satisfactorily shown that most if not all the fierce contests of parties during our national history have grown out of, directly or indirectly, the doctrine of state sovereignty. To name only a few great questions related to that doctrine—the slavery question, the protective tariff, internal improvements, currency and financial questions—these and other agitations came from diverse views of the powers of the general government.

A communication from Athens to the Atlanta Constitution states that on Wednesday last a remarkable event transpired. Three young farmers from Watkinsville went into a saloon to eat a watermelon. They put the melon down on the table rather hard, when to their astonishment it exploded with a loud noise and sent fragments flying in every direction. A large piece struck one of the party in the eye, and it is thought he will lose it, as the organ is very much injured. No one can account for the explosion. The melon must have been loaded with dynamite, probably for the purpose of frightening off depredators on the patch in which it was grown.

The truth of the maxim that "honesty is the best policy," was strikingly exemplified in Decatur a few days since. The DeKalb News says: "A negro man brought in from the country a fine looking lot of watermelons and offered them for sale on the streets. Johnny Scruggs bought one, cut it open and round it green. He went back to the negro and asked him to replace it. This the melon man refused to do and the fun began. Scruggs took his stand beside the melons, with a half of the green melon in his hand and warned all comers against buying, exhibiting his as a sample of the lot. Saturday was a public day at the Mountain and melons were in demand, but so successful was Scruggg's plan that only two or three were sold during the entire day. 'From early morn till dewy eve' Scruggs nursed his wrath and watermelon, and turned scores, if not hundreds, of would be buyers. A crowd gathered around the spot and whenever a new man turned away, cheered the plucky boy and laughed at the annoyed darkey. The latter offered to replace the melon that proved bad, or return the money: but the silent testimony of the green sample was powerful and they wouldn't sell. — When we left late in the afternoon, all things remained in statu quo—the melons unsold, the crowd hilarious, the negro mad and anxious, and Scruggs serene and persistent."

Young Buck, of Texas, who tried to kill John G. Thompson's son, has been re-appointed a cadet at West Point.
A nine-year-old boy in Bowie county weighs 130 pounds and measures thirty-nine inches round the chest.
Forty miles of iron for the Transcontinental road has been purchased. The extension is to be made west of Sherman.
A Sherman man made a bet of $100 that Dr. Tanner wouldn't hold out for forty days. He paid it Saturday afternoon.
Joe Blackburn, the man who killed Special Policeman Charles Scott at Gainesville, has been bound over in the sum of $5000.
At Chappell Hill the cotton worms are destroying the cotton fast, and farmers are trying to destroy the worms with arsenic.
San Antonio is the second largest city in the state, and the Express is happy, while the Houston Age is correspondingly dismal.
The fruit shipments of Denison this year will foot up in the neighborhood of 40,000 boxes. Not a good year for fruit either.
It is stated that the cotton worm is doing great damage to the crop in the upper part of Fort Bend and lower part of Waller counties.
Last Saturday Drs. Williams and Pitts of Sherman extracted from a man in that city a tape worm 302 feet long—so the Sherman papers say.
At Gainesville Saturday a cowboy's horse, escaping from its owner, ran full speed against the end of a wagon tongue and killed itself almost instantly.
The cotton crop of San Saba is booming; some persons predict a yield of one and a half bales per acre. In many places there is no signs of worms.
The cotton worms have appeared in various portions of Montgomery county, but, up to date, have done but little damage. Planters have used Paris green to stop them.

The Pittsburg Magnet got into a drunken row not long since and was shot in the knee and missed an issue. It says hereafter it will be careful how it gets into free fights.

The Gatesville Sun states that if the cotton crop of Coryell county turns out as it now promises to, the labor now in the county will not be able to pick it out and save more than half of it.

There are 225 counties in Texas. Of these 154 are unorganized. In 1878, 154 counties voted for Governor. Since then nine counties have been organized, making in all 164 organized counties.

One day last week a man named Edwards stole a wagon and pair of mules from a Mr. Wickel, who lives about three miles northwest of Paris, Lamar county. Wickel's wife eloped with Edwards.

Tuesday five prisoners escaped from the Houston jail. Among them were the celebrated Odell brothers, John and James. This is the third time they have escaped, and they boast that no jail in Texas can hold them.

W. M. Goss, a well-to-do freedman, living near Tyler, was shot in the breast and seriously injured Tuesday by his son-in-law, John Jeffers, who was intoxicated. Sheriff Butler captured the assassin and lodged him in jail.

Near San Antonio Saturday night four men and a boy, at the point of a pistol, robbed Ed Tewes' store, east of there, of $1000. Two of the robbers were caught in San Antonio the next night. The officers expect to get the remaining three.

The wheat crop of southwestern Burget has averaged very well. Mr. Roper, at Marble Falls, has so far threshed out some 5000 or 6000 bushels for his neighbors, with several thousand more engaged. The average per acre is five or six bushels.

On Sunday evening, in Houston county, a young man named Gabriel, while riding a wild horse near the residence of Mrs. Aiken, was thrown against a stump and killed. His ribs on one side were crushed in and he only survived a few minutes.

The preliminary examination of the case of the State v. W. P. Allen, charged with killing Deputy Sheriff Garrett, at Brenham, has been concluded. The justice decided to hold the defendant in a bond in the sum of $2500, to await the action of the grand jury.

Sunday night, on the Tehuacana, twelve miles from Waco, three men rode from the bushes and surrounded Mr. J. A. Foreman, who was traveling, and with drawn pistols compelled him to hold up his hands. They then took from him twenty-two dollars and passed on.
